summary: BELTAID is an autonomous wearable safety belt for lunar (0.16g) and Martian (0.38g) missions, powered by an ESP32 and MPU6050 sensor. Using a gravity-calibrated dual-threshold algorithm and power-saving architecture, it detects accidental falls without false alarms from normal hopping. Bypassing up to 44-minute Earth communication delays, BELTAID triggers immediate on-suit alarms and broadcasts automated SOS coordinates to nearby crewmates and habitats—protecting astronauts from proven low-gravity fall hazards (27 Apollo incidents) within seconds.
details:
The "BELTAID" (Autonomous Fall Detection and Local Emergency Telemetry System) for an astronaut in Reduced-Gravity Conditions.

1. Abstract

The astronauts in the Moon 0.16g and Mars 0.38g have a very high biomechanical risk for Extra-Vehicular Activities (EVAs). Bulky pressurized spacesuits can affect the astronaut's centre of gravity, cause the astronaut to have poor visibility from the helmet, and impact on the astronaut's balance, which is directly hazardous to the astronaut as well as the Portable Life Support Systems (PLSS). In addition to this risk, there can be a communication delay between the planet and the satellite, ranging from 2.6 seconds on the Moon to 44 minutes on Mars, thus rendering Mission Control unable to intervene with the satellite in real time. In this paper, a lightweight and autonomous wearable safety belt (BELTAID) for reduced gravity exploration is presented. Together with an MPU6050 6-axis Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) and an ESP32 microcontroller, BELTAID has a dual-threshold algorithm and gravity calibration, which are used to decide whether a fall is dangerous or just walking in space and performing a normal locomotion step. The system provides local audio-visual warnings for a fall, if detected, and automatically generated distress telemetry, including local positioning coordinates, to nearby crew members and habitat bases, with an interrupt-driven system to provide multi-hour EVA power endurance.

The problems presented here are mainly taken from historical sources.Most of the problems here have been adapted from the history.

Uneven planetary regolith and craters decrease space wear postural stability and traction in rigid spacesuits. Unlike Orbital Microgravity, Partial Gravity is not entirely eliminated by the falling astronaut and for the astronaut, it can be a very physical task to return to the surface. There were 14 falls and 13 near falls reported on NASA Apollo missions as they walked around on the moon (no crashes or fatalities were recorded):

On the Apollo 16 (1972) mission, Charles Duke lost his balance while jumping and hit his PLSS backpack with his back, which presented a risk of failure of the primary oxygen tank and cooling tank.

Problem on Apollo 16 (John Young, 1972): tripped over an instrument cable, broke a scientific experiment, and punctured the suit.

Face-first into the lunar regolith was the landing of Apollo 17 (Harrison Schmitt, 1972) which had to struggle to get out unaided, and to use up much of his oxygen doing it.

Due to astronomical distances, it is impossible to directly coordinate rescue operations from earth and the planetary crew must be able to detect and alert themselves locally instantly.

Designing a system that minimizes energy usage and increases efficiency.Architecture System & Power Optimization.

BELTAID is a modular hardware which will be powered by a 3.7V rechargeable Lithium battery with TP4056 protection circuit and be integrated into an unobtrusive waist belt. The MPU6050 IMU is used to get linear acceleration and angular velocity data, which is then used by an ESP32 microcontroller to fuse the data in real-time. The ESP32 will use light sleep cycling, waking up only when abnormal motion is detected, and low-power local RF/LoRa telemetry and positioning modules are only powered when an emergency is confirmed. While the short buzzer/LED activation is in progress, there is a grace window for manual SOS activation and false-alarm cancelation with a tactile push-button.

3. Methodology for fall detection using gravity.

The low gravity and longer fall phase when using a booter makes it impossible to use regular fall detectors found on the ground. BELTAID's algorithm scales according to the planetary gravity factor, which is 0.16 for the Moon and for Mars is 0.38:

The total increases above 2.5 times within 800, as well as the tilt shift of the gyroscope is larger than 60.

4. Conclusion

In reduced gravity, the potential for a fatal fall is shifted from a dangerous event to a quick and prompt crew rescue thanks to the combination of gravity calibrated inertial sensing, interrupt driven efficiency and efficient autonomous local telemetry achieved by BELTAID.
